author: Alyx Gorman explains it to Emma Joyce
description:
First introduced in 1991, ‘Maybe she’s born with it’ is out the door – but is the new slogan a glow-up?

Alyx, I hear a certain makeup brand has updated its tagline. Why is this a big deal?

The jingle that has been burned into the minds of women around the world since its Christy Turlington-helmed debut in 1991, “Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline”, has received what has being described as a “modernisation”. In a new campaign with Miley Cyrus, the “she’s” will be replaced with “we’re”, which both changes the observer’s perspective to something a little more self-directed and makes it more inclusive. But it’s a punctuation change that is raising eyebrows.

Continue reading...
title: Maybe it’s a new tagline. Maybe it’s more punctuation. Maybelline’s 35-year-old slogan has an update

author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agencies
description:
Lawsuit filed in California claims drivers routinely refuse to transport individuals with service animals or mobility devices

The Department of Justice sued Lyft on Monday, accusing the ride-share giant of discrimination for denying service to passengers with disabilities.

The federal lawsuit, which was filed in the US district court for the northern district of California, said Lyft drivers have routinely refused to transport individuals who depend on service animals or use mobility devices, such as wheelchairs, an alleged violation of the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA).

title: US justice department sues Lyft over alleged refusal to serve passengers with disabilities

author: Tom Garry
description:
Manchester City’s European campaign finally came roaring into life as they put four goals past Inter to record their first Women’s Champions League victory of the season and greatly improve their prospects of reaching the knockout stages.

The English side had to come from behind after a slow start but two goals from Aoba Fujino put them ahead before half-time, and second-half efforts from Kerstin Casparij and Grace Clinton gave them a 4-1 victory in Monza that doubled their points tally, after their draws against Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain.

description:
Legal battle escalates as far-right US podcaster continues to spread false claims that France’s first lady was born a man

Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron have brought a fresh defamation lawsuit against Candace Owens in her home state of Tennessee, in an escalation of a transatlantic legal battle as the far-right US podcaster continues to spread false claims that France’s first lady was born a man.

The Macrons first sued Owens and her media companies in July 2025 in Delaware in response to what the French first couple called “verifiably false and devastating lies” being repeated by Owens on her podcast and on X. According to that lawsuit, those lies included that Brigitte Macron, 73, was born a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her older brother – and committed

author: Associated Press
description:
Estranged father of Duchess of Sussex was arrested for keeping child sexual abuse material, authorities say

The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, just days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California, authorities said on Tuesday.

Thomas Markle was in custody awaiting a hearing in federal court in Tampa, Florida, first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said.

author: David Batty
description:
Arrests made after three properties were searched in relation to inquiry into late businessman

French police have made arrests after raiding three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, in relation to an investigation into sexual abuse and trafficking by Mohamed Al Fayed.

Several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released, according to the Paris public prosecutor’s office. Another property in Paris and one in Saint-Tropez, both with links to Fayed, were also searched in mid-October.

Continue reading...
title: French police raid Ritz hotel in Mohamed Al Fayed sexual abuse investigation

author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
description:
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has mandate to try to form a government – with Netanyahu waiting if he fails

Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in, deploying their majority to seize control of the legislature from Benjamin Netanyhau and his allies.

Although they are still too divided to form a government, the opposition requested a vote for a new speaker, who sets the Knesset’s agenda. Once Netanyahu loyalist Amir Ohana has been replaced, the six opposition parties will be able to work on key legislation even if they broker a coalition.

Continue reading...
title: Israeli opposition hurries to seize control as new Knesset is sworn in

  • No 1 pick Mendoza set to make first NFL start

Kirk Cousins is heading back to Minnesota.

Defense secretary calls impeachment effort a ‘farce’ and praises president in press conference for audience of one

There was no talk of “weirdos or beardos” – two among several categories whom Pete Hegseth has made it known are unwelcome in the US armed forces under his watch.

But a man with a beard had to be uppermost in his mind for him to meet journalists in the Pentagon at the ungodly hour of 8am on Tuesday.

Continue reading...
title: Hegseth lays it on thick for Trump to shave off fallout from Iran war

author: Editorial
description:
The judge took the suicide risk seriously while defending investigative journalism and the right of women to tell their stories

The Guardian and ITV News investigation into David Walliams has exposed difficult dilemmas for journalism. Last week, the high court helped clarify how to navigate them. The court heard that women had described to the Guardian how Mr Walliams, one of Britain’s most successful comedians and children’s authors, used his fame to prey on them for sex when they were young adults or teenagers. Publishing their claims carried a serious risk that Mr Walliams might take his own life. But this is a story of great public interest, and those women deserve to be heard. Some of them told the Guardian that they have lived with the effects of his alleged conduct for years.

For months, the Guardian and ITV News weighed concerns for him a
title: The Guardian view on David Walliams: allegations about abuse of power and sexual misconduct deserve publication | Editorial

author: Natricia Duncan, Joshua Surtees and Kejan Haynes
description:
Jason Jones welcomes decision by privy council in London to overturn 2025 ruling that outlawed anal sex

A gay man has won a historic 10-year battle against Trinidad and Tobago’s homophobic laws with a landmark UK appeals court ruling that could help overturn similar anti-gay laws in other Caribbean countries.

The privy council, based in London, overturned a 2025 decision by Trinidad and Tobago’s court of appeal that recriminalised consensual anal sex, seven years after the Trinidadian activist Jason Jones secured a high court judgment declaring the country’s colonial-era “buggery” laws unconstitutional.

Continue reading...
title: Activist wins 10-year fight against homophobic Trinidad and Tobago laws

  • Qatar and Abu Dhabi races set to go ahead as planned

Imola has been stood down as a back-up plan for the Formula One season finale as the sport pushes ahead with its scheduled Middle East races.

The Italian venue, 20 miles from Bologna, was lined up to replace Abu Dhabi as the final race amid concern over the ongoing conflict in the region.

Continue reading...
title: F1 presses ahead with plan to hold season finale in Middle East despite safety concerns

author: Alan Evans
description:
From Agatha Christie to a new generation of crime writers, cryptic crosswords have long held a place in murder-mystery fiction. Debut novelist and Guardian crossword setter Alys Cummings explains why the two make such natural companions

• Don’t get Cluesletter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

A cryptic crossword and a murder mystery are each bound by an unspoken agreement between the creator and reader: I will give you enough information to solve this, but you must put the pieces together yourself.

So it’s no wonder that crime writers, from Agatha Christie to Dorothy L Sayers, and TV shows, from Inspector Morse to Inside No 9, have been drawn to the puzzles in their stories. The latest writer to enter the cruciverbalist crime arena is Alys Cummings, whose debut novel, Murder Most Cryptic, was published in October.

Upside-down
title: Why murder mysteries and cryptic crosswords go hand in hand

author: Richard Luscombe
description:
Jason Leon Watford said he ‘snapped’ after verbal dispute with the woman, before allegedly killing her in a cabin

A passenger of a Texas-based cruise ship has been charged with murdering a woman in their cabin on Sunday on the first day of their voyage.

Crew members aboard the MSC Seascape found the unidentified victim deceased and face down on the cabin floor, with Jason Leon Watford sitting in a corridor outside scrolling through his phone, according to an FBI affidavit that details the alleged crime.

Continue reading...
title: Texas man charged with murder of woman aboard MSC cruise ship

description:
German chancellor has signalled he will block budget with no aid deal, complaining that burden is ‘carried mostly by only a few member states’

Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month.

The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort.

Continue reading...
title: Merz accused of ‘blackmail’ by Slovak PM after demand for Ukraine aid in EU budget

author: Robert Booth in Lisbon
description:
XPeng says its $300k low-altitude device will soon be ready for emergency services and recreational use in rural areas

People could start taking trips in flying cars in China as soon as next summer, the manufacturer of a two-seater vehicle with autopilot model has said.

Deli Zhao, the chief executive of the Chinese flying car company XPeng, said the $300,000 (£225,000) low-altitude device would be ready for use by recreational users in rural locations and by emergency services in the second half of 2027. After 10 years of development including trials of flying motorbikes at the company’s Guangzhou base, it has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.

Continue reading...
title: Flying cars could launch in China next summer, maker of two-seat model says

author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor

Claude chatbot developer had been reported to be aiming for $2tn IPO on Wall Street before investors cooled on AI

Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.05tn) in its imminent stock market flotation, short of the $2tn that had been expected before investors started to question the durability of the AI boom.

The developer of the Claude chatbot was widely reported to be targeting a $2tn initial public offering on Wall Street but its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday.

title: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation

US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterizing the interest as mutual.

United are expected to sack their head coach, Michael Carrick, after a disastrous start to their season which leaves them at risk of relegation from the Premier League, their worst opening to a campaign in four decades.

description:
Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities

author: Joshua Geer
description:
Academics are slowly piecing together the financial networks behind the transatlantic trafficking of ‘human cargo’

While the UK government is considering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, Lloyd’s of London said it was “deeply sorry” six years ago. The historic insurance marketplace said it was deeply sorry for the “significant role” it played in the trafficking of enslaved people and for the enormous suffering caused. It has since installed a commemorative plaque at its London headquarters.

Perhaps more consequential was the research that followed. Through an independent collaboration with Johns Hopkins University in the US, researchers Alexandre White and Pyar Seth examined Lloyd’s archives.

Continue reading...
title: Historians uncover more questions for insurers over their role in the slave trade

author: Ariana Baio
description:
New statue titled The Foot Soldier was installed on the National Mall just two days before Veterans Day

A new statue mocking Donald Trump was installed on Washington’s National Mall on Monday, this time poking fun at bone spurs that the US president was diagnosed with, which allowed him to defer the Vietnam war draft.

Just two days before Veterans Day, the gilded statue – titled The Foot Soldier – appeared near the National Gallery of Art’s Sculpture Garden. Created by the Secret Handshake, a group of anonymous artists, the statue depicts Trump sitting down while rubbing his bare foot.
title: Gilded statue in DC mocks Trump for ‘dodging’ Vietnam war draft over bone spurs

Crystal Palace could avoid having to pay Pierre Sage significant compensation if he is re-appointed by former club Lens, with the Frenchman’s departure from Selhurst Park still yet to be confirmed.

author: Daniel Boffey in Hamburg
description:
Sea Lion project in the North Falkland basin threatens to deepen sovereignty dispute

Argentina has told an international tribunal that Britain’s approval of oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has dramatically deepened a sovereignty dispute that led to war four decades ago.

At the start of an historic legal clash at the Hamburg-based International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos), an Argentinian legal team argued that the oil project must be suspended.

description:
• Age-gap relationship generated intense scrutiny

  • Hudson says clip invaded her privacy

Jordon Hudson is suing two Airbnb hosts over a Ring doorbell camera video of a bare-chested Bill Belichick. Hudson says that the 2023 clip invaded her privacy by prompting public disclosure of her relationship with the former New England Patriots head coach.

Hudson, who went on to become a public presence by Belichick’s side, says in the lawsuit that the pair were keeping their romantic relationship private when they stayed at the Boston-area rental in the summer of 2023. However, the doorbell video – which showed a shirtless Belichick stepping out of the home – emerged that fall and soon made the rounds in the media.
title: Jordon Hudson files lawsuit over shirtless video of Belichick that helped disclose romance

description:
Finals have hit California desert after stormy few years and pre-tournament kerfuffle has added to the fun

Towards the end of a positive day for Mirra Andreeva, one of the brightest young stars of women’s tennis, the 19-year-old approached the broadcast cameras to dissect her excellent 6-4, 6-0 win over Elina Svitolina in her first match at this year’s WTA Finals. Andreeva took her place alongside Madison Keys, the 2025 Australian Open champion and a guest reporter for Sky Sports at Indian Wells, who greeted her with a mischievous smile: “Hey, diva!” Keys said.

This was an obvious reference to the kerfuffle on the eve of the tournament, when Jessica Pegula, usually known as one of the most congenial players on the tour, had been caught on a hot mic delivering a series of stinging criticisms about Andreeva in a private conversation with her coach. Peg
title: Hot mics, Andreeva ‘diva’ drama and a stopgap finale at Indian Wells bail out the WTA  | Tumaini Carayol

author: Richard Luscombe in Miami
description:
The SS United States will sink off Florida coast to become an artificial reef, ending long-running wrangle over its fate

Final preparations were under way on Tuesday to sink the world’s fastest ocean liner in the Gulf of Mexico as an artificial reef, concluding a decades-long wrangle over the fate of the transatlantic icon.

A fleet of five tugboats moved the rusting hulk of the SS United States from a quayside in Mobile, Alabama, on Monday for its short journey to 25 miles off the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be scuttled in a precision operation on Wednesday afternoon.

Continue reading...

description:
The Japanese film-maker doesn’t hold back in his rendition of the 1963 film, with an epic battle that remains one of the most impressive action scenes in history

Within the first 20 minutes of Takashi Miike’s 13 Assassins, there is brutal murder, ritual suicide and political corruption, all taking place in Edo period Japan.

The film’s central villain, Lord Naritsugu – the Shogun’s half-brother, played with an almost ethereal detachment by Gorô Inagaki – has a taste for depravity that knows no bounds. At the beginning of the film, he slaughters the family of a local lord with such sadistic cruelty it pushes the justice minister, Sir Doi (Mikijirô Hira), into enlisting a samurai, Shinzaemon Shimada (Kōji Yakusho), to assassinate Naritsugu.

description:

While vaping is known to cause lung damage, breathlessness and nicotine addiction, the singer and actor Selena Gomez has posted in a video on Instagram that vaping has permanently changed her voice.

“Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you’re going through it, or if you’re even trying to vape, it’s just not worth it,” she said. “It’s so stupid and it changed my voice. I’m not going to be able to change my voice. I vaped a lot.”
title: Selena Gomez says vaping has changed her voice. Can e-cigarettes really affect your vocal cords – and is it reversible?

author: Julia Kollewe
description:
GLP-1 products such as Ozempic and Mounjaro spread but many in poorer countries struggle to get basic diabetes treatment

The gold rush into GLP-1 weight-loss drugs risks diverting pharmaceutical firms’ attention away from diabetes treatments such as insulin, the head of the Access to Medicine Foundation has warned.

GLP-1 blockbuster medications such as Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro have revolutionised obesity and diabetes treatment but there has been a greater focus by companies on weight loss, according to a report from the Netherlands-based non-profit group.

• F10 unions fear financial loss if they play in second tier

  • Promotion/relegation set for 2030 Nations Championship

The Six Nations and Sanzaar are facing another battle with World Rugby over a desire from some unions to ensure that none of them can be relegated from the Nations Championship.

As reported last week by the Guardian, the 10 leading unions have set up a new company, F10, to run the Nations Championship and sell their broadcast and commercial rights for all competitions other than the World Cup, which remains the property of the global governing body, World Rugby.

author: Molly McCluskey in Skagway, Alaska
description:
Skagway’s 1,100 permanent residents are caught between a boom time – when the ships bring more than a million tourists – and a lull in winter

October comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left.

The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. Soon, they will all be gone. Snow is visible on the nearby mountains.

Continue reading...
title: This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?

As the nights draw in, many of us can experience low mood. But for a small proportion of people a more intense depression develops through the winter months. It’s a phenomenon that since the 1980s has been labelled seasonal affective disorder, or Sad, and can be debilitating for sufferers. To find out more about the latest scientific understanding of Sad, Ian Sample speaks to Russell Foster, professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford. He explains what scientists think the mechanism for the condition could be and what the evidence says about the best way to tackle it.

description:
Multiple women allege David Walliams abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were young women, an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. He denies the allegations.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on this investigation, Walliams writes: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He adds: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
title: The allegations against David Walliams | Investigation by the Guardian and ITV News

The warning signs were all there, but I blithely scanned the QR code without a second thought

‘Hey hey, Zomo!” read a text from my sister, and I should have immediately smelled a rat. We never spell it “hey” – always “hej”, after the Swedish friend who taught us how to say “hey” in Swedish, in 1984. And “Zomo”, obviously, is not my name, although it represents me in her contacts list – the “mo” indicates “mobile”, dating back to a time (let’s call it 1994) when we would mainly use a landline. Also, she only uses an exclamation mark where it’s absolutely necessary: for instance, “What a jerk!”

That opener was so out of character I should have called her immediately to check she hadn’t been kidnapped. Instead, I read on: “Could you please vote for Mia? She is my friend’s daughter, and the grand prize is money for her education – every vote counts. Thank you!”

description:
Some say their plants are fine without fertiliser, but are they just surviving when they could be thriving?

The problem
Enter a garden centre and you will be overwhelmed by a wall of feeds: liquid concentrates, slow-release, droplet bottles and specialist formulas for every plant going. Many people swear by them, while others say they have never fed their plants and they’re doing just fine. After all, plants in the wild manage perfectly well. So do our houseplants genuinely need feeding, or is it just consumerism?

The hack
Plants get energy from photosynthesis, but not minerals. They come from the soil, and in a houseplant bound by its pot that supply runs out over time. In the wild, roots roam through soil, fed constantly by decaying leaves, rain and living organisms. Adding fertiliser gives your plants the nourishment they need to grow and thrive.
title: Houseplant hacks: do you really need to feed your plants?

Was the failed assassination of the Polish pope a Soviet plot or simply the work of a deranged hitman?

At 5.17pm a man pulled out a concealed pistol and raised it with both hands above the heads of the crowd. He took aim at the pope, only a few metres away, and fired several shots. Then, as he backed away from the shocked bystanders, he tripped and fell, where he lay pinned to the ground by a Franciscan nun until handcuffed by uniformed police. description:
Based on a 2003 memoir, this remarkable documentary shows the incredible bravery these young men showed in the face of battle and unrelenting bigotry

Here is the remarkable story of the US army’s “Soul Patrol” unit in the Vietnam war: the all-Black Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol (or LURP), a six-man team of largely teenage African American soldiers, within Company F 51st Infantry. Their duty was to go behind the Vietcong enemy lines, each carrying 150lbs of kit and an M16 assault rifle, and in conditions of terrifying danger report on the enemy’s movements. One heart stopping anecdote is about a panicky member of the unit, who had never seen fireflies before, and became convinced he had seen a Vietcong insurgent in the undergrowth, smoking a cigarette. The film also reports on their later, poignant reunion as old men, using their contemporary home-movie footage and dramatically recreating some scenes.

This is the last day of a DIY language course that I devised when Rouen’s language schools told me they were full for the only week I could get away. This turned out to save me a pretty penny: language school tutors cost €60 an hour while Anna – who I discovered on the website Apprentus – is a cost-effective €19 an hour.

Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.
title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen

author: Clare Clark
description:
The unlikely friendship between French and English composers Maurice Ravel and Ralph Vaughan Williams has inspired a tender and generous novel

In 1907, composer Ralph Vaughan Williams confided to the critic Edwin Evans that he was finding his own music “lumpy and stodgy”. His musical education at the Royal College of Music, and indeed classical music in England in general at that time, had tended towards the Teutonic – Bach, Brahms, Beethoven, Wagner – and their heavy contrapuntal style dominated his work. To free himself, he told Evans, he planned to spend some months studying under French composer Vincent d’Indy, who taught at the Paris Conservatoire. Evans’s colleague, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi, had other ideas. He proposed that, rather than the traditionalist d’Indy, Vaughan Williams should take lessons with his close friend Maurice Ravel, by then one of the most admired young composers in France.

The two men could hardly have been more different: Ravel pet
title: Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan Coe review – what can music tell us about national identity?

author: Guardian Staff
description:
From the Specials and the Beat to Paul Weller and Sade, Janette Beckman’s glorious black and white photographs perfectly captured British music in the late 1970s and early 1980s

Continue reading...
title: One step beyond! Janette Beckman on her era-defining 2 Tone and ska images – in pictures

author: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent
description:
Seven films in Seville programme highlight how Roma are creating their own narratives

Growing up in Romania, whenever Alina Șerban spotted Roma people on television or in movies, they were usually cast as villains or depicted as somehow exotic.

But this week the Romany actor and film-maker is part of a cohort pushing back against this stereotyping, joining forces with Romany film-makers from across Europe in a landmark screening of seven films during the Seville European film festival.

Continue reading...
title: ‘We are human too’: the Roma film-makers striking back at stereotypes

author: Reuters
description:
The reported evacuation comes weeks after the US withdrew bombers from RAF Fairford over a suspected Iran-linked security incident

The US military evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in ⁠Britain on Monday after a threat from Iran, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing people familiar with the matter, weeks after Washington withdrew its bombers from ⁠RAF Fairford airbase over ⁠a suspected Iran-linked ​security incident.

Two US refuelling tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base diverted to Germany earlier on Monday, while several other tankers at the base ⁠were moved to Germany and other locations later in the day, the WSJ report said.
title: US reportedly evacuated aircraft from RAF Mildenhall over Iran threat

author: Helena Kennedy
description:
Workers in music, film, TV and theatre may not feel they can speak up about abuse, but the authority I lead is able to help them

  • Helena Kennedy KC is a Labour peer and the chair of the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority

Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in jail yesterday, after being convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. The details that emerged from his case have been shocking and at times deeply disturbing. We have witnessed the bravery of the women who came forward to seek justice – and the brazen and brutal sense of entitlement exhibited by a pampered star at the height of his fame.

The Brand trial brought into sharp relief many of the victim-blaming attitudes I have spent my professional life as a criminal barrister trying to challenge. Old tropes emerged about victims not screaming out during rape and not reporting immediately. This is why lawyers who conduct sex cases should be
title: Russell Brand’s conviction won’t end abusive behaviour in the creative industries, but at least whistleblowing is now possible | Helena Kennedy

author: Miatta Mbriwa and Patrick Butler
description:
Worthing is at the centre of a growing revolt against branch closures that charity leaders say are vital to its future

Seven years ago, Samaritans volunteers Mark and Carol saved a stranger’s life. On the other end of the phone was a “very distressed” man. He had climbed scaffolding to the top of a building and was threatening to jump.

As Mark talked to him, Carol called his local Samaritans to alert volunteers. Eventually the man came down off the scaffolding and they “walked” him street by street to safety.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Is anyone up for a fight?’ The battle for the soul of Samaritans

author: Emma Graham-Harrison Chief Middle East correspondent
description:
Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power, even as they struggle to form government

Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.

High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.

Continue reading...
title: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel’s PM

author: Lisa O’Carroll
description:
Jens Eskelund says Europe may need to allow its companies to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains

Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.

In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

Continue reading...
title: EU manufacturers could give up on competing with China by 2030, warns commerce chief

author: Rukmini Iyer
description:
A filling vegetarian curry, with leftovers to stuff into a wrap or pie. The same sauce can also be used as the base for a matar paneer. Cook once, eat thrice!

You can’t beat a creamy, tomato-based curry when you’re in need of comfort food, although chilli aficionados might want to up the amount of crushed red chillies from one teaspoon to two – or more. This takes on even more flavour by roasting one of its star ingredients – cauliflower – in spices, before adding it to the sauce with some good jarred butter beans (you can use tinned, but you might want to simmer them for an extra 10 minutes, so they take on more flavour).

Continue reading...
title: Rukmini Iyer’s recipe for cauliflower and butter bean malai curry | Cook once, eat twice

author: Rob Smyth, Will Unwin and Sachin Nakrani
description:
Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it

The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure.

***
title: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number

author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
description:
Exclusive: Iran war has fuelled energy price rise and clouded outlook, driving up unemployment, says Clare Lombardelli

Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.

Continue reading...
title: Young people in UK hit by ‘low-gear economy’, warns Bank of England deputy

author: David Wingrave
description:
Established in UK cities for decades and much loved for their green plumage, the Himalayan birds have been recast as an ecological threat. But is the idea of invasive species itself a problem?

Before we saw a single parakeet, we heard them: a disembodied static that grew louder as we approached Hither Green cemetery in south-east London. It was an early evening in late June, and we had come to witness an invasion. By the time my friend and I reached the cemetery’s western edge, the clamour was all-encompassing. We hopped the fence and picked our way through the gravestones. Above us now were the birds themselves, their kryptonite-green plumage, scab-red beaks, pearly black collars and trailing tail feathers unmistakable: Psittacula krameri, the ring-necked parakeet.

Hither Green cemetery hosts one of the city’s largest roosts. Every day at dusk, a sizeable chunk of London’s feral parakeet population returns here, to a specific line of poplars. They like to spen
title: Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets

author: Shefaa’ Al-Qudah
description:
In a country of severe water scarcity, the Abu Obeida mosque in Deir Alla captures ablution wastewater before it reaches the sewers to use for irrigation

The Abu Obeida mosque in Deir Alla, Balqa, to the west of Amman, stands in one of the hottest and most arid stretches of the Jordan valley. Yet an oasis of trees and flowerbeds surrounds it, improbably green against a landscape of bare ochre hills, watered by drip irrigation lines that run along the ground between the roots.

The water does not come from the municipal network, but from the taps where worshippers wash their hands, faces and feet before prayer.

Continue reading...
title: How a Jordan mosque is recycling ritual water to create a green oasis

author: Emine Saner
description:
Last year, two men opened fire on a Jewish community in Sydney – and Ahmed Al Ahmed risked his life to disarm one of them. The man’s accomplice then shot him five times. He describes what he was thinking in those fateful moments, and what happened next

When he heard the loud cracks, one after another, Ahmed Al Ahmed’s first thought was that they were fireworks. But he was confused – it was still daylight. It was his cousin who realised they were gunshots, and shouted at him to run and hide. “We ended up hiding between two cars,” Al Ahmed remembers. It was like “hell”, he says, “something like the end of life. I can hear very heavy shooting, nonstop, and people screaming – women, kids, everyone.” He could feel his heart pounding and hear his rapid breathing.

By the time it was all over, 15 people, including a 10-year-old girl, were dead, and many more wounded, shot by two gunmen who opened fire on a Jewish community celebrating Hanukah at Bondi beach in Sydney. A 16th vi
title: Shots rang out. I hid behind a car. Then I wrestled the gun from the Bondi beach shooter

author: Andrew Roth in Washington
description:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe

US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.

The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.

Continue reading...
title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin

author: Tim Jonze
description:
He thinks painting is futile, the YBAs were an embarrassment, and most artists today might as well be working in carpet shops. So why is his new show full of, er, paintings? We meet the confounding British artist

‘This is so bad isn’t it?” says Ryan Gander, grinning like a naughty schoolboy. “People are going to hate me when you write this up.” The 50-year-old conceptual artist has just finished telling me why, not only does he dislike drawing or painting, he finds the very act “futile and dumb”. He explains: “Copying reality with a pencil and paper just seems completely mad to me. It’s such a weird act. Why would I draw you when I could just take a photograph?”

Gander has many such opinions, from how we measure the value of work to why 90s Brit art was a load of nonsense (more on that later). He also has a superb way of communicating that makes whatever he says seem like the most obvious thing in the world. After an entertaining couple of hours in his company, I
title: ‘It was hard coming after the shallow, egocentric YBAs’: brilliantly bolshie artist Ryan Gander lambasts practically everyone

author: Jack Snape
description:
With the issues raised in Cape Town still to be resolved, Usman Khawaja’s book threatens to damage reputations and divide cricket’s tight community

Australian cricket thought it had left its great shame behind, burying it in the days after Cameron Bancroft was shown on the big screen in Cape Town putting sandpaper down his pants.

Cricket Australia acted swiftly at the time, suspending the young batter, his captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner. Too swiftly, according to Usman Khawaja, whose book released on Tuesday criticised the investigation while Warner called it “rushed and botched”.

Continue reading...
title: The saga that never goes away: wounds of Australian cricket reopened as ball tampering resurfaces | Jack Snape

author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
description:
Beekeepers say they are fielding a record number of calls from people needing assistance in removing swarms

Engulfing parked cars and blanketing inner-city street signs – New Zealand’s largest city, Auckland, is in the midst of an unusually large bee swarming season, that experts say has been exacerbated by a milder than usual winter.

The Auckland Beekeepers Association says it is fielding five to 10 calls a day, requesting assistance to remove swarms of bees – with individual members of the association being contacted for help as well.

Continue reading...
title: Auckland hit by swarms of bees after milder than usual New Zealand winter

author: Dara Kerr
description:
Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars

California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth.

The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”.

Continue reading...
title: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth

description:

Russia’s battlefield losses have reached levels unprecedented in its modern

author: Agence France-Presse
description:
Political rivals lead crowd starting from city’s market square where attack unfolded while mourners stop at memorial for six people killed

Tens of thousands of people joined a silent march in Kraków on Monday evening, led by Poland’s president and prime minister, in tribute to the victims of a mass shooting that shocked the country over the weekend.

They set off from the city’s historic market square, where the attack unfolded on Saturday afternoon. Mourners stopped at a flower-covered memorial marking the spot where the gunman opened fire from his car, killing six people and wounding 15 others.

Continue reading...
title: Polish leaders join thousands at silent march in Kraków for mass shooting victims

author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
description:
Boy says he was first exposed to extremist material on TikTok, turned to Telegram and YouTube for bomb-making instructions, and used ChatGPT to devise his plans

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A teenager who admitted to planning a terrorist attack in Sydney in 2024 has told the court he was radicalised online after first seeing extremist material on TikTok and used ChatGPT to form his plans.

The 16-year-old, known under the pseudonym as RK due to his age, pleaded guilty to acts in preparation for, or planning, a terrorist act. In a sentencing ruling on Monday, he avoided jail time, with the New South Wales supreme court ordering him into a three-year community corrections order.
title: Teenager who planned terror attack in Sydney tells court he was radicalised online and used AI to strategise
